description: Fifty-two (52) laminar smoke points were measured aboard the ISS in non-buoyant round-jet diffusion flames in co-flowing air across five fuel compositions (C2H4, C3H8, C3H6, 75% C3H6/25% N2, 50% C3H6/50% N2), whereas methane (CH4) did not reach a smoke point before the flame impinged on the downstream copper screen at the end of the duct.
phenomenon: Laminar smoke point threshold in microgravity co-flowing jet diffusion flames

reported_values.author_interpretation: All observed smoke-point flames were attached to the burner (not lifted). Ethylene testing was limited by fuel supply depletion (two 150 cc bottles at 760–1440 kPa gauge).
reported_values.experimental_or_computational_context: Experimental microgravity flight tests in ISS MSG across 526 total ignited flames (12 sessions, Feb–June 2009); burner IDs 0.41, 0.76, 1.6 mm; co-flow velocities 5.4–65 cm/s.

description: Two distinct visual flame tip behaviors occur at the smoke point in microgravity depending on fuel luminosity: propane and ethylene exhibit gradual dimming, reddening, and rounding of the luminous flame tip, whereas bright flames (propylene and propylene/N2 mixtures) exhibit a rapid transition to open-tipped flames with centerline flame extinguishment and an annular shell of escaping soot.
phenomenon: Open-tipped flame extinction and soot escape morphology at smoke point

reported_values.author_interpretation: Open-tipped flames are common in microgravity when smoke points are far exceeded, associated with radiative heat loss causing flame extinguishment along the centerline and reactant/soot leakage.
reported_values.experimental_or_computational_context: Experimental visual and digital still/video observation of attached co-flow laminar jet diffusion flames in microgravity.

description: For a fixed fuel flow rate, decreasing co-flow air velocity increases luminous flame length until the smoke point is exceeded, after which luminous length decreases due to tip extinction. Conversely, for a fixed fuel and burner diameter, increasing co-flow air velocity moves the smoke point to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous smoke-point flame lengths.
phenomenon: Co-flow velocity effect on luminous flame length and smoke point length

reported_values.author_interpretation: Increasing co-flow velocity decreases centerline residence times and radiative heat-loss fractions, delaying soot escape and lengthening the smoke-point flame. Flame length is more sensitive to fuel flow rate than co-flow velocity because excess oxidizer is available.
reported_values.experimental_or_computational_context: Experimental measurements across co-flow velocities 5.4 to 65 cm/s and burner diameters 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm.

description: In microgravity co-flowing flames, smoke-point luminous flame length decreases with increasing burner inner diameter (smaller burners yield longer smoke-point lengths). When extrapolated to zero co-flow velocity, the dependence on burner diameter diminishes.
phenomenon: Burner diameter scaling of non-buoyant co-flowing smoke-point flames

reported_values.author_interpretation: Attributed to residence time effects because fuel jet velocity scales as d^-2 at constant fuel mass flow rate; higher jet velocities from smaller nozzles reduce residence time and radiative loss fraction. Note that 0.41 mm burner tests (propylene only) showed day-to-day repeatability scatter.
reported_values.experimental_or_computational_context: Comparison of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm inner diameter nozzles in co-flowing air, compared against quiescent microgravity data (Urban et al., 2000).

description: Measured microgravity smoke-point luminous flame lengths scale empirically with burner diameter and co-flow air velocity as L_SP proportional to d^(-0.91) * u_air^(0.41), and correlate linearly with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction (m_dot_f / Z_st) via L_SP = 1.6097 * (m_dot_f / Z_st) with R^2 = 0.9514 (with flames having u_a/u_f < 0.08 lying slightly above the correlation).
phenomenon: Empirical scaling laws for non-buoyant co-flow smoke-point flame lengths

reported_values.evidence_type_as_extracted: Calculated/empirical regression result from experimental data
reported_values.author_interpretation: Consistent with stoichiometric flame length theory where smoke point occurs at roughly twice the stoichiometric flame length, though centerline residence time models alone failed to produce a universal quantitative correlation.
reported_values.experimental_or_computational_context: Regression analysis of 52 measured smoke-point conditions across all tested hydrocarbon fuels and burner sizes.

description: Based on smoke-point flame lengths at fixed burner diameter and co-flow velocity (and pseudo threshold soot index estimates), the sooting propensity of the tested fuels in microgravity increases in the order: ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene (with an exception on the 0.76 mm burner where ethylene exhibited a longer smoke-point length than propane). This reverses the normal-gravity ranking between ethylene and propane.
phenomenon: Anomalously high sooting propensity of propane in microgravity diffusion flames

reported_values.author_interpretation: Propane exhibits an unusually high sooting propensity in microgravity compared to normal gravity; lower density of ethylene reduces residence time, though authors note this alone is unlikely to fully explain its long smoke point on the 0.76 mm burner.
reported_values.experimental_or_computational_context: Comparison of smoke-point lengths and pseudo-TSI across fuels in microgravity vs normal-gravity apparatus results.

description: Cold-flow anemometer mapping at 18 duct locations and COMSOL numerical simulations show that the co-flow air velocity profile inside the SPICE duct is spatially non-uniform, exhibiting a pronounced centerline velocity deficit (center-dipping wake) at the 13 mm downstream station caused by the nozzle boundary layer, which partially persists at the 56 mm station.
phenomenon: Nozzle wake and boundary layer distortion in co-flowing duct flow

reported_values.evidence_type_as_extracted: Direct experimental observation and numerical simulation result
reported_values.author_interpretation: A minimum DC voltage is applied to the fan even at dial setting 0 to prevent fuel accumulation; actual velocity with a flame is further altered by thermal expansion and cannot be directly measured due to MSG diagnostic space limits.
reported_values.experimental_or_computational_context: Pre-flight hot-wire/omni-directional anemometer measurements across 6 fan dial settings (0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10) and 2D axisymmetric COMSOL simulations for 1.6 mm ID nozzle (50 cm/s jet velocity; 0, 25, 100 cm/s co-flow).

source_section: B. Air velocity distribution in the flow duct
